subtype: Different ways of relating in toddlerhood [Actor]
passage:
"Mridul! Mridul!" Papa called. Mridul kept lining up his cars along the sofa edge, red, blue, red, blue.
"He's not ignoring you," said Mahima, his mother. "He's busy."
"And last night he screamed when we did bath before dinner."
"He likes the same order. But look." Mridul toddled over and pressed his forehead against Mahima's knee, then went back to his cars.
"That's his hug," she said softly. "I've booked the paediatrician for Friday, just to ask."

qa.q: What was Mridul lining up along the sofa edge?
qa.a: He was lining up his cars, red, blue, red, blue.

qa.q: What does Mridul pressing his forehead against Mahima's knee suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he feels affection and comfort with his mother, showing love in his own way instead of a usual hug.

qa.q: What is a sensible next step for parents with concerns like Papa's?
qa.a: Notice and describe the behaviours calmly, as Mahima does, and ask the paediatrician, who can assess them.

qa.q: How does Mahima see Mridul's behaviour?
qa.a: She sees it with tender understanding; to her he is busy, not ignoring, and his forehead press is his hug.

grounding: Toddler Mridul lines up objects, responds less to his name and is upset by a changed routine, while showing love in his own way; his parents plan to ask a paediatrician.

passage:
"Vishal, do you know volcanoes have magma chambers? And lava can be as hot as a very hot oven, and some volcanoes are under the sea, and—"
"Yusuf, do you want to play blocks?" Vishal asked.
Yusuf sat down next to Vishal and built his own tower, talking about volcanoes the whole time.
"Now snack," said Miss Rao.
"No! First blocks, then story, then snack!" Yusuf covered his ears.
"Okay, Yusuf. Blocks, story, snack." He lowered his hands.
Later Vishal said, "Miss, Yusuf didn't play with me."
Miss Rao smiled. "He sat next to you all morning and told you his favourite things. That's his way of being friends."

qa.q: What order did Yusuf want for the morning?
qa.a: First blocks, then story, then snack.

qa.q: Why did Yusuf cover his ears when Miss Rao said snack?
qa.a: He felt upset and anxious because the order he needed for his day was changing.

qa.q: How could an adult help Vishal understand Yusuf?
qa.a: Like Miss Rao, they can explain that sitting close and sharing favourite things is Yusuf's real way of connecting.

qa.q: How might Vishal feel after Miss Rao's explanation?
qa.a: Vishal might feel less left out and see that Yusuf was being friendly, just differently.

grounding: Yusuf plays beside Vishal, talks at length about volcanoes and needs a set order for the day, and his way of connecting is real.

passage:
On the bus back from the district hospital, Kavitha held Ayesha, five, on her lap. The doctor had said Ayesha's mind worked differently and named some therapy at the town centre.
Kavitha stared at the fields. Was it the phone she had let her watch? Her chest felt heavy. Ayesha hummed and traced circles on the window, over and over.
Kavitha kissed the top of her head, hard. Mine, she thought.
That Saturday, at a mothers' meeting behind the panchayat office, another woman said, "My son is the same. The therapist taught us picture cards." Kavitha wrote everything down.

qa.q: Where was the mothers' meeting held?
qa.a: Behind the panchayat office.

qa.q: What was Kavitha feeling on the bus home?
qa.a: She felt worried and guilty, wondering if the phone had caused it, but also a fierce love as she kissed Ayesha's head.

qa.q: What helped Kavitha start supporting Ayesha as she is?
qa.a: Meeting other mothers who shared practical ideas, like the therapist's picture cards, and following up with professionals.

qa.q: What is it like for Ayesha on that bus ride?
qa.a: She seems calm and absorbed, humming and tracing circles, safe on her mother's lap.

grounding: Kavitha feels worry, guilt and fierce love after learning her daughter thinks differently, and connecting with other families and professionals helps.

subtype: Social rules that are not obvious [Actor]
passage:
In the school playground in Uppsala, Leila stood still while the others ran. "You're it!" Oskar shouted, tagging her as he ran past. Leila frowned. She had not agreed to be anything.
Later in class, Ms Ulla said, "Leila, pull your socks up, your spelling is slipping." Leila bent down and pulled up her socks. Two boys laughed. Leila's face went hot; she didn't know what she had done wrong.
By three o'clock, the scraping chairs and shouting felt like sandpaper in her head. She put her head on the desk.
Ms Ulla crouched beside her. "I'm sorry, that was a saying. I meant please try harder with spelling. Next time I'll say exactly what I mean." She drew the tag rules as three pictures on a card. Leila studied them, and her shoulders dropped a little.

qa.q: What did Leila do when Ms Ulla told her to pull her socks up?
qa.a: She bent down and pulled up her socks.

qa.q: How did Leila feel when the two boys laughed?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and confused, her face hot, because she didn't know what she had done wrong.

qa.q: Which of Ms Ulla's choices worked, and why?
qa.a: Apologising, saying exactly what she meant and drawing the rules as pictures helped far more than any telling-off, because Leila could understand clearly.

qa.q: How might Oskar see Leila standing still after he tagged her?
qa.a: He might think she was being unfriendly or odd, without knowing the game's rules just weren't clear to her.

grounding: Leila takes words literally, finds playground rules confusing and is exhausted by school noise, and clear, kind explanations help her.

passage:
Monday. Leela noticed that Zubin never joined kho-kho. He sat on the steps, hands over his ears, and told anyone passing about the Rajdhani's engine numbers. Some boys called him Train Brain. Leela didn't laugh, but she didn't say anything either.
Thursday. Leela sat next to him. "Why don't you play?" she asked. "Too loud," Zubin said. "Trains are loud too, but I like that loud." Leela laughed. "Can you teach me the engine numbers?"
The next Monday. For the class project, Leela suggested making a railway map of India. Zubin drew every route from memory while three others coloured the stations. When Aryan said "Train Brain" again, Leela said, "He's our map expert, actually." Zubin didn't look up, but he was smiling.

qa.q: What did Leela suggest for the class project?
qa.a: A railway map of India.

qa.q: Why did Leela sit next to Zubin on Thursday?
qa.a: She was curious about him and a bit uneasy about staying silent while others teased him, so she wanted to ask rather than assume.

qa.q: What small steps helped Leela build a real friendship with Zubin?
qa.a: She asked why he didn't play, took an interest in his trains and planned a project around them, and stood up to the teasing.

qa.q: How might Zubin feel when Leela calls him the map expert?
qa.a: He probably feels proud and accepted, even though he doesn't look up, because a classmate valued what he loves.

grounding: Leela notices a classmate who avoids loud games and loves trains, asks instead of assuming, includes him through his interest and stops the teasing.

passage:
Neelam: Didi, are you home?
Ishita: Yes, in the kitchen. How was school?
Neelam: I did Riya's laugh all day. Practised the "haha omg" face in the mirror at lunch.
Neelam: Said "same" to everything.
Ishita: That sounds tiring.
Neelam: I'm SO tired. I'm going to come home and I can't talk. Please don't ask me anything. Please.
Ishita: Okay. Your room is dark, fan's on, headphones are on the bed. No questions till you're ready.
Neelam: Mummy will ask about the test.
Ishita: I'll tell her later. You don't have to perform here.
Neelam: Thank you.
Neelam: Can we just watch the train videos after dinner? Without talking?
Ishita: Yes. Silent train videos. Our thing.

qa.q: What did Neelam practise in the mirror at lunch?
qa.a: The "haha omg" face.

qa.q: How is Neelam feeling on the way home?
qa.a: Neelam feels completely exhausted and anxious about being asked to talk after a whole day of copying others to fit in.

qa.q: What did Ishita do that could help anyone in Neelam's place?
qa.a: She prepared a quiet, dark room, kept questions away and made home a place where Neelam doesn't have to perform.

qa.q: If you were Ishita, what might you want Neelam to know?
qa.a: That it is safe to be natural at home, and that loving Neelam doesn't depend on the laughs and faces used at school.

grounding: Neelam masks at school by copying a friend's expressions and scripts, arrives home exhausted, and her sister's acceptance gives a place to rest.

passage:
Thursday night
Chinmay joined our class two weeks ago. Everyone thinks he's rude because he doesn't look at you and never high-fives. Today at the lab table I asked him, "What's the easiest way for you to talk?" He took a long time. I waited. I counted to ten in my head and did NOT fill the silence.
Then he said, "Writing. And no touching, please."
So I wrote my question on the corner of the worksheet. He wrote back a whole paragraph about the reaction! He knows so much.
When the bell rang, he covered his ears. I didn't make a joke. I just said "bye" clearly and didn't wait for him to look up.
I really like him. I want to be the kind of friend who asks first.
Preeti

qa.q: How long did Preeti count in her head while waiting?
qa.a: Preeti counted to ten and did not fill the silence.

qa.q: What does Preeti's last line suggest about how Preeti feels?
qa.a: It suggests Preeti feels warm affection for Chinmay and admiration for how much he knows, and hopes to be a friend who asks first.

qa.q: What did Preeti do well, and why did it help?
qa.a: Preeti asked how Chinmay prefers to communicate, gave time to answer and respected his wish for no touching, so he could share his knowledge comfortably.

qa.q: How might Chinmay experience the lab lesson?
qa.a: He may feel relieved and respected, since he didn't have to force eye contact or high-fives and could talk in writing.

grounding: Preeti speaks clearly, waits for answers, respects Chinmay's sensory needs and asks how he prefers to communicate instead of treating difference as a defect.

passage:
14 Nov
Woke at 6:10. Tea, oats, same as always. The hostel was quiet, which is my favourite time.
Spent four hours in the library on moths. Did you know some moths navigate by the moon? I did not stop to eat. I forgot.
In the seminar, Rohan asked what I thought of his presentation. I said the second half didn't follow from the data. His face went stiff. I meant it as help. I need to remember people sometimes want a softer first sentence.
But then, at the nature club, a girl called Charu showed me her photo of a luna moth. We talked for an hour straight. She said, "Finally, someone who doesn't get bored." Same time next Friday.
Good day. Tired now. Earplugs in.
Sudha

qa.q: What time did Sudha wake up?
How did Sudha feel after the talk with Charu?
qa.a: Sudha felt happy and excited, having finally found someone who shared the same deep interest in moths.

qa.q: What could Sudha try next time someone asks for honest feedback?
qa.a: Keep the honest point but start with a softer first sentence, so the helpful meaning comes across.

qa.q: How might Rohan have felt about Sudha's comment?
qa.a: He probably felt stung and a bit embarrassed, even though the comment was honest and meant as help.

grounding: Sudha's deep passion, direct speech and need for routine and quiet show strengths of focus and honesty, and a friendship forms around a shared interest.

passage:
Sit, sit. You're new, so let me tell you about Naveen. Twenty years I've been in this firm, and I'm Ganga, the one who trained him.
Naveen joined at twenty-four, sharp as anything with code. But the open floor wore him out. The chatter, the phones, the Monday small talk. By four o'clock he'd be staring at the wall. His first manager called him moody.
Then one day he came to me with a typed page. "I work best with written tasks, a quieter desk and clear deadlines. Is that possible?"
Honestly, I was surprised. But I asked the manager, Suresh, to try it. Naveen moved to the corner near the server room. Suresh sent every task in writing.
Within a month, Naveen's work was the cleanest on the team. He told me, "Being understood is like putting down a heavy bag." Remember that, if you ever need to ask.

qa.q: Where did Naveen move his desk?
qa.a: To the corner near the server room.

qa.q: How did Naveen feel once the changes were made?
qa.a: He felt relieved and lighter, saying being understood is like putting down a heavy bag.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Naveen's typed request for written tasks, a quieter desk and clear deadlines; asking for reasonable adjustments let his real skills show.

qa.q: How might Suresh have seen Naveen after a month?
qa.a: Suresh probably saw him as one of the strongest people on the team, not moody, once the tasks were clear and written.

grounding: Ganga tells a new colleague how Naveen found the open office and small talk draining, asked for adjustments and thrived with written tasks.

passage:
"Pema, why is your reading book under the cupboard?" Vasudha Miss asked after class.
"I lost it."
"It's right there."
Pema looked at the floor. "The words jump. B and d keep swapping. Everyone reads fast and I'm stuck on 'bridge'."
"That sounds really hard."
"I'm stupid, Miss."
"Pema, who told the whole story of the lost yak yesterday, with all the reasons why it ran away?"
"Me."
"Stupid children can't do that. Your brain is fine. Reading is just the tricky bit for you."
"So what do I do?"
"We start tomorrow: ten minutes with me each morning, bigger print, and a finger under each line. And I'll ask your parents about getting some extra help, early."
Pema pulled the book out from under the cupboard.

qa.q: Which word did Pema say was a sticking point?
qa.a: Pema said the word 'bridge'.

qa.q: Why did Pema hide the reading book?
qa.a: Pema felt ashamed and discouraged, because the words jump and Pema had started to believe being stupid was the reason.

qa.q: How did Vasudha Miss protect Pema's confidence?
qa.a: She reminded Pema of the strong storytelling about the yak, separated intelligence from reading, and started patient daily help plus early extra support.

qa.q: How might Pema's parents feel when Vasudha Miss talks to them?
qa.a: They might feel worried at first, then relieved that a teacher noticed early and has a plan.

grounding: Pema, a bright child who hides books and feels stupid, learns from the teacher that intelligence is intact and reading is the difficulty, with early, patient help.
